story.logline: You drive to work each day and wonder if an e-bike would help; charging seems to cancel the gain, yet per kilometre it emits a few percent of the car, so what does switching change?

question: Should I ride an e-bike to work instead of driving?

source.title: Car or e-bike for the daily commute?
source.publisher: Test fixture written for this repo, illustrative numbers
quotes: A typical petrol car uses about 7 litres of fuel per 100 kilometres.
Burning a litre of petrol releases about 2.3 kilograms of carbon dioxide, so each kilometre adds about 160 grams of CO2.
An e-bike uses roughly 1 kilowatt hour of electricity for every 100 kilometres: about one hundredth of the energy.
On an average grid, a kilowatt hour causes about 0.5 kilograms of CO2, so an e-bike kilometre causes about 5 grams.
A kilowatt hour costs around 30 cents.
For a 10 kilometre commute each way, five days a week, 46 weeks a year, the car burns about 320 litres of petrol a year and emits about 740 kilograms of CO2.
The e-bike uses about 46 kilowatt hours.
They don't: even counting the electricity, the e-bike emits a few percent of the car's CO2 for the same trip.
An e-bike costs around $2,500 and needs servicing.

explain.caption: Car or e-bike for your commute? Follow one trip to work.
Every workday, your car carries you there and back.
To move you, your car burns petrol you pay for.
Each litre burned puffs carbon dioxide, CO2, into the air.
An e-bike can take some trips, so the car does fewer.
Its battery charges from the grid. Making power makes CO2 too.
But per kilometre, charging makes a few percent of the car's CO2.
So the petrol you don't buy stays in your pocket.
Savings build up until they cover the e-bike's price.
Rain, heavy loads and long trips may still send you by car.
Now make it yours. Your commute decides the rest.

simulate.prompt: Try your own distance, car and petrol price.

tradeoffs: An e-bike costs around $2,500 up front, but each trip after that costs very little to power.
Keeping the car covers heavy loads, bad weather and long trips, but its other costs stay with you.
Riding every trip cuts the most CO2 and petrol, but asks the most of you on hard days.
leftOut: E-bike servicing: the article says it needs servicing but gives no cost, so check what applies to you.
Car costs other than petrol, such as insurance, servicing and parking, which may change little if you keep the car.
The CO2 from making the e-bike and its battery, which the article gives no figure for.
How clean your own grid is: the model uses the article's average of 0.5 kg of CO2 per kilowatt hour.
Prices change. The petrol and power prices here are the article's illustrative figures, so check your own.
questionsToAsk: What servicing does this e-bike need, and what does it usually cost each year?
How far does the battery go on one charge, and how many years does it last?
Is there a safe route and somewhere secure to leave the bike at work?
Would my car insurance or registration cost change if I drove less?
